content: The earliest documented instance of cremation rites involved cremation followed by burial in a tumulus, resembling the Urnfield burial tradition. This description, however, is somewhat anachronistic, as burial was the predominant practice during Mycenaean times. Homer’s references to cremation in the Iliad may reflect the more widespread use of cremation in the later period when the epic was composed. Criticism of burial practices has often been a point of contention among competing religions and cultures. Cremation, in particular, has been associated with fire sacrifices or even human sacrifices. Hinduism and Jainism are notable for not only permitting but prescribing cremation. In India, cremation is first evidenced in the Cemetery H culture (circa 1900 BCE), which is considered a formative stage of Vedic civilization. During this period, ancestors were invoked as either cremated (agnidagdha) or uncremated (anagnidagdha). Cremation was common, though not universal, in both Ancient Greece and Ancient Rome. According to Cicero, inhumation was regarded as the more archaic rite in Rome, while cremation was typically reserved for the most honored citizens, particularly the upper classes and members of imperial families. Christianity opposed cremation, influenced by Jewish tenets and as part of an effort to abolish Greco-Roman pagan rituals. By the 5th century, cremation had nearly disappeared from Europe. In early Roman Britain, cremation was common but declined by the 4th century. It re-emerged during the Migration Era in the 5th and 6th centuries, often involving the inclusion of sacrificed animals and the dressing of the deceased in costumes and ornaments for the pyre. This practice was widespread among the Germanic peoples of northern continental Europe, from whom the Anglo-Saxon migrants originated. The ashes were typically deposited in clay or bronze vessels within urn cemeteries. However, this custom faded with the Christian conversion of the Anglo-Saxons in the 7th century, when inhumation became the general practice. During the Middle Ages, cremation was forbidden by law in parts of Europe and was even punishable by death if combined with heathen rites. Authorities sometimes used cremation as a form of punishment for heretics. For example, the body of John Wycliffe was exhumed years after his death, cremated, and his ashes were thrown into a river as posthumous punishment for his denial of the Roman Catholic doctrine of transubstantiation. On the other hand, mass cremations were often conducted out of necessity, such as after battles, pestilence, or famine, to prevent the spread of contagious diseases. Retributory cremation persisted into modern times. After World War II, the bodies of 12 men convicted of crimes against humanity at the Nuremberg Trials were cremated, and their ashes were disposed of in a secret location to prevent their use as memorial sites. In Japan, however, a memorial building was allowed for the remains of many executed war criminals who were also cremated. Similarly, some Communist countries used cremation as an aggravated form of capital punishment, with the ashes of the executed disposed of ignominiously to further humiliate their families. Even today, cremation carries a stigma in many former Socialist countries, where it is often viewed as a shameful or dishonorable practice. In the modern era, cremation gained renewed attention in 1873 when Professor Brunetti of Padua presented a cremation chamber at the Vienna Exposition. In Britain, the movement was supported by Queen Victoria’s surgeon, Sir Henry Thompson, who, along with colleagues, founded the Cremation Society of England in 1874. The first crematoria in Europe were built in 1878 in Woking, England, and Gotha, Germany. In North America, the first crematorium was established in 1876 by Dr. Francis Julius Le Moyne in Washington, Pennsylvania. The second cremation in the United States occurred in Salt Lake City, Utah, in 1877. The first cremation in Britain took place on March 26, 1886, in Woking. Cremation was declared legal in England and Wales following the prosecution of Dr. William Price for cremating his son. Formal legislation followed with the Cremation Act of 1902, which imposed procedural requirements and restricted the practice to authorized locations. Some Protestant churches came to accept cremation, reasoning that God can resurrect a bowl of ashes just as conveniently as He can resurrect a bowl of dust. However, the 1908 Catholic Encyclopedia criticized these efforts, associating them with Freemasonry and describing them as a sinister movement, though it acknowledged that cremation was not directly opposed to any Church dogma. In 1963, Pope Paul VI lifted the ban on cremation, and in 1966, Catholic priests were permitted to officiate at cremation ceremonies. Australia also embraced the modern cremation movement, establishing its first purpose-built crematorium and chapel in 1901 at the West Terrace Cemetery in Adelaide. This small building, resembling those in Woking, remained largely unchanged in style and operational until the late 1950s. The oldest operating crematorium in Australia is at Rookwood in Sydney, which opened in 1925. In the Netherlands, the Association for Optional Cremation was founded in 1874, sparking a long debate about the merits and demerits of cremation. Laws against cremation were challenged and invalidated in 1915, though cremation did not gain legal recognition until 1955. During World War II, the Nazis constructed and operated massive crematoria within their concentration and extermination camps to dispose of the bodies of thousands of Jews, Romani people, and other prisoners who were killed or died daily in the camps.
